content: Neonatal hypotension that does not respond to volume expansion, catecholamines, or corticosteroids is associated with a mortality rate of approximately 50%. Optimizing blood pressure and ensuring adequate tissue perfusion in cases of refractory hypotension is critical to improving clinical outcomes. Vasopressin, a neuropeptide hormone, and its synthetic analogue, terlipressin, have been utilized in the treatment of refractory hypotension in neonates and may offer therapeutic benefits. The primary aim of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of vasopressin and its analogues, such as terlipressin, in reducing mortality and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, as well as improving survival rates in neonates with refractory hypotension. Secondary objectives included evaluating the effects of these agents on blood pressure improvement, increased urine output, reduction in inotrope scores, and the incidence of complications such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular hemorrhage, chronic lung disease, and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). A comprehensive literature search was conducted in January 2012 using the Cochrane Neonatal Group's recommended search strategy. The search included electronic databases such as CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library), MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE, as well as abstracts from the Pediatric Academic Societies and trial registries like ClinicalTrials.gov and Controlled-Trials.com. References from identified articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized trials that evaluated vasopressin or its analogues at any dosage or duration, used as an adjunct to standard therapies (including volume expansion, inotropic agents, and corticosteroids) for the treatment of refractory hypotension in neonates. Standard Cochrane Collaboration methods were employed for the systematic review. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies based on titles and abstracts, obtaining full-text versions when necessary. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Electronic forms were designed for trial inclusion/exclusion, data extraction, and requests for additional information from study authors. The search did not identify any completed or ongoing trials that met the inclusion criteria. Three studies were excluded because they did not involve neonates, and one study was excluded because its objective was not to treat refractory hypotension in neonates. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of vasopressin or its analogues in the treatment of refractory hypotension in neonates. To address this gap, well-designed, adequately powered, randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy, optimal dosing, safety, and long-term neurodevelopmental and pulmonary outcomes associated with these treatments.
